_comment: 微型指南英文正文。键 = guides/<文件名> 去 .md（与 terms.en.json 同一套路）。值形如 {lead, points[], myth, fact}。

怎么向 AI 提问.lead: The same question asked differently produces very different answers. This guide covers the five things to state before you ask.
points: State the goal and the done-criteria: not "write an article" but "write a 300-word intro for absolute beginners".
Give context: who you are, who the audience is, and what constraints apply — length, format, tone.
Paste the source text into the conversation; don't make the AI guess which passage you mean.
Ask for an outline first: have it list the structure, you approve it, then expand.
When unhappy, point out exactly what is wrong — more effective than a vague "try again".

怎么验证 AI 的输出.lead: AI will state fabricated facts with full confidence. This guide turns "what it said" into "what you can check".
points: Break the output into individual checkable claims: numbers, dates, names, citations.
For every citation (paper, statute, API name), verify at the original source — never trust the title it gives you.
Demand sources for key numbers; treat numbers without sources as assumptions.
Self-review catches only a fraction of errors; cross-checking (different source, different tool) is what works.
The more specific the domain (local law, your own data), the more a human must check — general models don't have these facts.

AI 真的读懂了你的话吗.lead: A fitting answer is not understanding — it is doing something else.
AI 真的读懂了你的话吗.myth: It answers aptly and keeps up with the conversation, so it must have understood what you meant.
AI 真的读懂了你的话吗.fact: Language models generate text from context. A fitting response shows task behavior; fluency alone does not establish understanding of your situation. Check references, constraints and preserved facts.

参数越多就越聪明.lead: Parameter count is one variable, not a dial for intelligence.
参数越多就越聪明.myth: Parameter count decides how smart a model is — bigger is always stronger.
参数越多就越聪明.fact: Data, architecture, training methods and task also affect performance. Compare models under equal task conditions rather than treating parameter count as a quality score.

通用人工智能快到了.lead: "Soon" is a claim, not a verifiable milestone.
通用人工智能快到了.myth: Everyone says AGI is near, so there must be a checkable date when it arrives.
通用人工智能快到了.fact: AGI definitions and evaluation criteria are not settled. A claim of proximity needs specified capabilities, test conditions and completion criteria; a research goal or forecast does not establish achievement.

它说得笃定，所以可信.lead: Fluency and correctness are separate; a confident tone adds no reliability.
它说得笃定，所以可信.myth: A confident tone and a tidy structure mean the content is trustworthy.
它说得笃定，所以可信.fact: Confident wording alone does not establish correctness. Check support for each claim, especially numbers, dates, names and citations; leave unverified parts unknown.

温度调高会更聪明.lead: Temperature changes randomness only, not how much the model knows.
温度调高会更聪明.myth: Raising temperature makes the model more imaginative, therefore smarter.
温度调高会更聪明.fact: Where supported, temperature affects sampling rather than adding knowledge. Check output diversity and task correctness separately, and consult the actual interface for applicability and range.

它记得你之前说过的.lead: What it can see is the context window; anything outside is not in its input.
它记得你之前说过的.myth: Within one conversation it always remembers everything said earlier.
它记得你之前说过的.fact: Generation uses context supplied for the request; a product may also retrieve history or store preferences. Cross-session retention and deletion depend on the product, not on one correct continuation.

榜单分数高就是好用.lead: A benchmark covers only what it measures — your task is a different question.
榜单分数高就是好用.myth: A model that scores high on the leaderboards must also be good at your task.
榜单分数高就是好用.fact: Leaderboard results depend on tasks, versions, setup and metrics. They inform initial screening, not your inputs, latency, failure costs or permission constraints. Scores on different bases are not directly comparable.

上下文窗口越大越好.lead: Window size has a price; enough beats maximum.
上下文窗口越大越好.myth: The larger the context window, the better long documents get handled.
上下文窗口越大越好.fact: A stated context window describes capacity, not equally effective use of every passage. Longer input can add memory use and latency. Compare evidence coverage, answer quality and cost for the task.

它拒绝，是因为做不到.lead: Most refusals are a trained choice, not a capability ceiling.
它拒绝，是因为做不到.myth: When it says "I cannot do that", it lacks the capability.
它拒绝，是因为做不到.fact: A refusal may reflect policy, permissions, input conditions or capability limits. Inspect the reason and applicable rules instead of inferring capability from one refusal.

它逐字读懂你的文字.lead: What it sees is not characters but ids from a vocabulary.
它逐字读懂你的文字.myth: It reads your input word by word, the way you do.
它逐字读懂你的文字.fact: Text is typically tokenized; tokens and words/characters need not map one-to-one. For exact counting, spelling or punctuation, define rules and use checkable methods rather than inferring accuracy from conversation.

它在一步步推理.lead: The steps it writes are not guaranteed to be the path that produced the answer.
它在一步步推理.myth: The reasoning it shows you is the reasoning it actually performed.
它在一步步推理.fact: Generated steps can be checked but need not fully expose the computation producing an answer. Verify conditions, observable steps and results; a coherent explanation is not a substitute.

注意力就是它注意到重点.lead: Attention is a weighted computation, not the model paying heed.
注意力就是它注意到重点.myth: "Attention mechanism" means it picks out what matters, like a person would.
注意力就是它注意到重点.fact: Attention weights are computational quantities, not direct equivalents of human attention or causal explanations. Visualizations aid observation; conclusions still need controlled checks or other validation.

量化会让模型变笨一半.lead: The impact varies by tier; the ruler is bits per weight.
量化会让模型变笨一半.myth: Quantising cuts model quality in half.
量化会让模型变笨一半.fact: Quantization changes numeric representation. Effects depend on model, method, tier and task. Bits per weight describe average storage, not capability; compare quality, memory and speed on equal tasks.

显存不够就跑不了.lead: Whether it runs and how fast it runs are two questions.
显存不够就跑不了.myth: If it does not fit in VRAM, the only option is a better graphics card.
显存不够就跑不了.fact: Some runtimes support system-memory/CPU offload, subject to total memory, architecture and speed constraints. Budget weights, cache and runtime separately before assessing smaller variants, quantization or offload.

接口兼容就等于行为一致.lead: Compatibility guarantees the shape of requests and responses, nothing more.
接口兼容就等于行为一致.myth: If the API is OpenAI-compatible, switching over gives the same behaviour.
接口兼容就等于行为一致.fact: Compatibility typically concerns specified request/response conventions. Check supported scope, defaults, streaming, tools and errors individually. Shared interface names do not establish equal behavior or output quality.

预览版不能用于生产.lead: Judge it by the terms and the timeline, not by the word "preview".
预览版不能用于生产.myth: Anything labelled "preview" is an experiment and cannot go to production.
预览版不能用于生产.fact: The preview label alone does not decide permitted use. Check intended-use permission, support/availability commitments, retirement and migration. Keep undisclosed details unknown.

开源模型一定更省钱.lead: Open guarantees the right to use and modify, not that it is free.
开源模型一定更省钱.myth: Once a model is open, running it is necessarily cheaper than calling an API.
开源模型一定更省钱.fact: Self-hosting still needs hardware, maintenance, monitoring and review, and actual license conditions matter. Compare total costs at equal workload and quality rather than equating free download with free use.

换模型只是改个名字.lead: A compatible interface does not mean a zero-cost migration.
换模型只是改个名字.myth: Switching models is just changing a name in the config.
换模型只是改个名字.fact: Configuration may change by one line while prompts, tools, parsers, quality, cost and data terms change materially. Compare representative inputs and retain rollback before declaring migration complete.

怎么保护自己的数据.lead: Before handing material to an AI, be clear about where it goes and what it leaves behind. Six moves.
points: Sort material by whether it may leave: personal identity, company secrets, and customer data are three different categories.
Do not accept terms you cannot read; check specifically whether your data is used for training.
Anonymize first: strip names, IDs, and contact details before pasting anything in.
Assess local/private deployment for sensitive work, while checking outbound model calls, telemetry, plugins and logs.
Afterwards, check retention: can the chat history and uploaded files be deleted, and how soon?
Set team rules: which materials may go into an AI, and which must stay in internal tools.

AI 常犯什么错.lead: AI mistakes follow fixed patterns. Recognizing these categories prevents most of them in advance.
points: Inventing facts: it produces plausible-looking fake citations, numbers, and dates.
Agreeing with you: imply a wrong premise and it usually will not correct it, just build on it.
Bad at exact math: precise counts, multi-digit arithmetic, and tricky date conversions fail most often.
Over-answering: it rarely says "I do not know", preferring a vague answer instead.
Swayed by phrasing: the same question asked differently can produce a different answer.

怎么读模型卡.lead: A model card is the manufacturer's spec sheet for a model. This guide covers which sections to read and which claims to discount.
points: Start with intended-use and limitations: what the maker says it is and is not good for beats marketing copy.
When reading benchmarks, first ask which ones were tested; a score without a benchmark is no score.
Read the training-data section: the data mix determines which biases it may carry.
Read the license: commercial use, attribution duties, and whether derivatives must share the same license.
Trust the known-limitations section: failure modes the maker admits are worth more than "state-of-the-art".
Compare vendors only on equal terms: same benchmark, same settings, or the numbers are not comparable.

怎么判断 AI 新闻是不是炒作.lead: AI news can omit test conditions or overstate scope. Check the original source, evaluation setup and unresolved claims before accepting a conclusion.
points: Find the original source first: a paper, an official announcement, or just a demo video. The longer the retelling chain, the more distortion accumulates.
Separate "demo" from "average": cherry-picked success cases are not everyday performance. Ask what the success rate is.
Ask about the measuring stick before reading numbers: only same-benchmark, same-setting comparisons count. A score jump after switching benchmarks is not progress.
Check the publisher's motive: a company mid-fundraise and an independent evaluator do not word things with the same reliability.
Look for independent replication. Results only the publisher measured itself should be treated as unconfirmed.
Discount timelines: "next year" and "will replace X in a few years" are predictions, not facts.

怎么防提示注入.lead: Prompt injection is an attack where outside content hijacks an AI. This guide covers how to build defenses so your AI tool treats web pages as data, not commands.
points: Treat outside content as data, not instructions: web pages, documents, and emails can hide "ignore your previous instructions".
Grant least privilege: if reading suffices, grant read-only; if one directory suffices, do not hand over the whole disk.
Keep a human gate on irreversible actions: deletions, transfers, and outbound messages ask a person first.
Isolate sessions: do not mix a session that processes outside content with one that holds keys or manages accounts.
Check what a tool can touch before installing it: read the MCP server's permission declarations.
Keep execution logs: when something goes wrong, you can replay what it actually did.

怎么给 AI 工具配权限.lead: How dangerous an AI tool is is mostly decided by the permissions you give it. This guide covers granting exactly enough and no more.
points: Decide the job first, then the permissions: coding work gets the code directory, not your whole home directory.
Grant read and write separately: if the task completes read-only, do not grant write.
Mark off-limits zones: key files, account configs, and system directories are explicitly excluded.
Turn on confirmation mode: deletions, overwrites, and outbound sends must ask before acting.
Reclaim permissions regularly: when a project ends or the task changes, take back what you opened.
Run experiments in restricted mode: try untrusted usage inside a sandbox first.

怎么安全地用 MCP 工具.lead: MCP lets an AI touch your files and the web. The tools themselves are not the danger; what gets fed to them and what permissions they hold is.
points: Install only the servers you need: every extra tool is one more channel something can go wrong through.
Read the permission declarations: file servers should scope to directories; fetch servers should carry security warnings.
Treat fetched content as data: web page text can contain instructions aimed at the AI.
Keep sensitive directories out: before connecting a file server, confirm keys and account configs are not inside.
Check who maintains the server: official and third-party carry different trust levels.
Cut the link first during an incident: if injection is suspected, stop the tool, then investigate the session.

怎么查生成式 AI 合规义务.lead: Launching an AI feature in China, compliance is not mysticism but a handful of checkable articles. This guide walks them in launch order.
points: Classify first: does the service face the public in mainland China? If so, the Interim Measures for Generative AI Services apply.
Check training-data provenance: Article 7 requires "lawfully sourced data and foundation models".
Check labeling duties: generated images and video must carry labels per the deep-synthesis rules.
Check filing: services with public-opinion attributes or social mobilization capacity need security assessments and algorithm filing.
Check the new labeling rules: the Labeling Measures take effect 1 September 2025 — explicit labels plus implicit labels in file metadata.
When unsure, ask legal: this site states what the articles say, it does not hand down legal conclusions for you.

怎么对照 EU AI Act 自查.lead: The EU AI Act sorts AI into four risk tiers, with obligations taking effect in batches. This guide covers how to classify yourself and which tier you hit.
points: Identify purpose, service region and provider/deployer role before checking scope. A minimal-risk label does not remove other laws or generally applicable duties.
Check prohibited practices under Article 5 together with their conditions, scope and exceptions. Names such as social scoring or biometric identification are not enough to decide applicability.
Transparency duties: chatbots must let people know they are talking to a machine; AI-generated content must be identifiable, and deepfakes visibly labeled.
Check general-purpose AI model duties against provider role, model circumstances, provisions and transition rules; do not treat all models/products alike.
High-risk duties are the heaviest: risk assessment, data quality, logging, and human oversight, none optional.
Watch the timeline: obligations take effect in batches, so the same product must meet different requirements on different dates.

怎么查 AI 生成内容的版权风险.lead: AI content copyright has two ends: whether the data fed in is lawful, and whether what comes out belongs to you. This guide checks both ends.
points: Input side, check provenance: Chinese rules require "lawfully sourced data and foundation models".
Input side, check exceptions: the EU Directive on Copyright in the Digital Single Market sets text-and-data-mining exceptions, with research and commercial terms differing.
Output side, do not assume ownership: whether AI-generated content can be copyrighted differs by jurisdiction; check local practice first.
Before commercial use, read the vendor terms: model terms of use differ on commercial use, competing products, and output ownership.
Keep provenance records: where materials came from and what the training data was — the chain of provenance comes first in disputes.
Litigation is ongoing: case law changes; for major commercial decisions consult legal counsel, not news headlines.

怎么读开源模型的许可证.lead: "Open source" does not mean use however you like. The conditions in a model license decide whether you may use it commercially, attribute, and what derivatives inherit.
points: Separate open-source software licenses from model licenses: the latter often carry extra conditions you cannot infer from the words "open source".
Check commercial terms: some licenses ban commercial use; others set a scale threshold.
Check attribution: Apache 2.0 requires keeping notices and the NOTICE file.
Check derivative duties: copyleft licenses require models you fine-tune to carry the same license.
Check use restrictions: many model licenses forbid certain use cases; violating them voids the license.
Check license inheritance: which license a fine-tuned, quantized, or merged model carries is recorded repo by repo in this site's model profiles.

怎么排查 AI 的数据泄露路径.lead: Data usually leaves you through more than one path. This guide lists the common leak paths one by one so you can check which ones you are on.
points: Input path: anything pasted into a cloud chat box has already left your device.
Training path: many services default to improving models with your conversations; find the opt-out switch.
Tool path: a connected server can carry content to its own backend.
Log path: how long chat history and uploaded files persist on the other side's servers.
Memory path: a model may repeat content it saw during training.
Recovery path: confirm the deletion entry point and effective time in advance; do not expect instant cleanliness.

怎么给 AI 内容做发布前检查.lead: Before publishing AI-generated content, a few classes of error appear almost inevitably. This guide is the pre-publication checklist.
points: Re-verify facts line by line: numbers, dates, and quotes — AI produces ones that look right.
Verify citations exist: paper IDs, book titles, links — open each one and confirm.
Run sensitive statements once more: sentences about people, organizations, or the law get rewritten in professional register.
Check image labels: add explicit labels per China's Labeling Measures; do not miss the implicit label in metadata.
Unify the voice: strip the AI register (parallel clauses, empty summaries) or readers will spot it instantly.
Keep a change record: which parts AI wrote and what you changed — traceable when something goes wrong.

怎么给文档做分块.lead: The first step of retrieval-augmented generation is cutting documents into chunks. How well you cut decides whether answers can be found at all.
points: Cut by meaning, not by character count: never slice a complete argument in half.
Chunks too small: context is lost, and even a hit cannot support a full answer.
Chunks too large: one chunk mixes several topics, and the similarity signal gets diluted.
A few hundred to a thousand characters is a common starting point; tune by results, do not trust a fixed value.
Overlap adjacent chunks: sharing a few sentences prevents information from breaking at the boundary.
Keep structural information: store titles, sections, and page numbers as metadata so retrieval can filter on them.

怎么给检索结果重排.lead: Retrieval returns candidates; reranking changes their order. Benefits depend on answer coverage, ranking quality and latency budget.
points: Coarse pass retrieves wide: pull dozens of candidates, not just the top three.
Fine pass switches models: a reranker compares query and candidate item by item, finer than vector distance.
Reranking has a cost: more candidates means slower and pricier; set the candidate count by your latency budget.
Check language support of the reranker: not every reranking model handles Chinese.
Tune top-k: fewer final items beats more — irrelevant chunks drag the answer off course.
Measure the two stages separately: coarse recall and fine ranking are scored apart, so you know which stage drags.

怎么做混合检索.lead: Vector search is good at similar meaning; keyword search is good at exact matches. Hybrid search merges the results of both paths.
points: Use keyword search or structured filters for exact model/ID conditions, while checking tokenization, spelling and indexed fields; keyword retrieval can also miss results.
Give fuzzy phrasing to vectors: a reworded question still hits, which keywords cannot do.
Fuse the two result lists: reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) merges by rank, not by force-adding scores.
Scores cannot be added directly: cosine similarity and BM25 scores have different scales; adding them skews results.
Check native support: hybrid queries are built into Qdrant and Weaviate.
Decide about reranking after fusion from quality and latency needs. Measure candidate recall and ranking instead of adding another model by default.

怎么挑 embedding 模型.lead: The embedding model decides how "similar in meaning" is computed. Pick it wrong and retrieval, reranking, and answering all suffer.
points: Check language support first: for Chinese tasks, read scores on Chinese or multilingual benchmarks; a good English leaderboard says nothing about Chinese.
Weigh dimensions against cost: higher dimensions usually mean pricier storage and compute; estimate by data volume.
Screen with benchmarks like MTEB, then test on your own data; the leaderboard is only a starting point.
Queries and documents must use the same model: vectors from different models have no meaningful distance.
Mind normalization: some models require normalized outputs before cosine similarity is valid.
Switching models means rebuilding the index: old and new vectors are incompatible; migration means recomputing everything.

怎么评测 RAG 的效果.lead: A RAG failure can come from retrieval or from generation. Evaluate them separately, or you will fix the wrong part.
points: Build an eval set first: real questions with gold answers; a few dozen is enough to start.
Retrieval side, measure recall: did the chunk that should be found make it into the candidates?
Generation side, measure faithfulness: can every sentence in the answer be supported by the retrieved chunks?
Measure answer relevance separately: on-topic answers with wrong grounding are still a problem.
Automate with a framework like RAGAS, then spot-check by hand to calibrate its scoring.
Break scores down by scenario: average scores hide the weak spots of specific question types.

什么时候不该用 RAG.lead: RAG is not the default. It fits "knowledge changes, citations required"; it hurts other scenarios, and forcing it makes things worse.
points: Small, stable knowledge: put it straight in the context; a retrieval layer is needless complexity.
Exact arithmetic or reasoning required: retrieval does not help; the limit is the model itself.
Poor document quality: garbage in, garbage out — fix the documents before talking about retrieval.
Tight latency budget: retrieval plus reranking plus generation is a long chain; weigh it for real-time use.
Strict consistency required: two runs of the same question may retrieve differently; assess this for compliance settings.
Try the baseline first: ask without retrieval; if it is good enough, do not build RAG.

怎么把提示词写结构.lead: "How to Ask AI" covers what to state before asking; this guide covers what shape to put it in: role, task, constraints, and format, written as separate blocks.
points: Write in blocks, not one wall of prose: role and background in one block, the task in another, constraints in another, output format in another — models follow blocked instructions more reliably.
Put standing rules (tone, boundaries) in the system prompt and the current task in the user message — each layer does its job; don't stuff one-off requests into the system prompt.

Mark sections with headings or tags (e.g. "Background:", "Requirements:"), and on long inputs clearly separate the material to process from the instructions, so the model doesn't treat data as directives.
Write constraints as checkable items: "under 300 words", "for absolute beginners", "cite sources" — these beat "shorter" or "more professional".
Give the output format its own block plus one worked example: a single sample output beats three paragraphs describing it.
Change one thing at a time when editing a prompt and compare results; change five at once and you can't tell which one worked.

few-shot示例怎么选.lead: Dropping a few input→output examples into the prompt changes performance noticeably — but bad examples steer the model the wrong way. Five criteria for picking them.
points: Cover the edge cases you actually need, not just the easy ones: the model imitates the distribution of your examples.
Keep the format identical to real inputs: field names, punctuation, and line breaks in the examples get copied verbatim.
Start with two or three examples; marginal returns drop fast, and too many crowd the context and raise cost.
Make examples differ from each other: three near-identical ones are worth one, and they teach the model it can only do that one thing.
When outputs go off the rails, first check whether an example is steering them — a wrong example is worse than no example.

思维链什么时候有用.lead: "Think step by step" helps some tasks a lot and barely helps — or actively hurts — others. How to tell whether extended reasoning is worth it.
points: Sort the task type first: arithmetic, multi-step logic, and planning gain a lot; simple extraction, translation, and format conversion gain almost nothing.
Trigger phrases like "think step by step" mattered for older models; reasoning models already have long chains built in, so prompting for one just wastes tokens.
Asking the model to list steps before answering works better — and is more controllable — than a bare "think about it".
Chain-of-thought output is not a reliable record of thinking: the model may fabricate a plausible-sounding process after the fact; don't treat it as an audit log.
Extended reasoning multiplies output length and latency; measure the cost before enabling it in real-time settings.
There is only one way to know if it helps: run a comparison on your own task, don't trust claims of "general improvement".

怎么让AI按格式输出.lead: When a program has to consume AI output, "please output JSON" often isn't enough. Three levels, from prompt-level constraints to structured outputs.
points: Level one: a format spec plus one complete sample in the prompt. Enough for most cases, but missing fields and stray commentary still happen.
Level two: use the API's structured-output / tool-calling capability — server-side constrained decoding guarantees valid format, far more reliable than asking nicely.
Define schemas with only the fields you need and tighten types: fewer fields, smaller failure surface.
Validate on the receiving end regardless of level: on schema-validation failure, retry or degrade — never feed downstream code unchecked.
Format constraints and task quality pull against each other: forcing a format can degrade content, so evaluate the two separately.
Don't let format tricks substitute for content evaluation: valid output is not correct output.

怎么自建评测口径.lead: Public leaderboards can't answer "is it good at my job". How to build an eval that is yours alone: questions, grading, and how to run it.
points: Collect questions from real failures: 20–50 inputs from your actual work beat copying a public benchmark.
Write down what counts as correct for each question: exact matching where there's a gold answer; a rubric — or a strong model grading against one — for open-ended ones.
Pin the question version and the input conditions (model, parameters, prompt), otherwise score changes have no explanation.
Separate the two error kinds: format errors (rule-checkable) and content errors (need a human or a model judge) — the fixes are completely different.
Run regressions: after swapping a model or editing a prompt, re-run the same set and watch which questions flip from right to wrong — flips to wrong deserve more attention than flips to right.
Watch for contamination: public benchmarks may sit in training data; your own questions dodge that, but rotate them periodically too.

榜单怎么读.lead: The myth page says a high leaderboard score doesn't mean it works well; this guide shows how to squeeze real information out of a leaderboard: who runs it, how it tests, and where it distorts.
points: Check three things first: who maintains it, where the questions come from, and how scores are computed — a leaderboard missing all three is an ad.
Look at when the questions were published: a benchmark only discriminates if it postdates the model's training cutoff; suspected-contaminated public sets inflate scores across the board.
Break the aggregate apart: the same model can rank completely differently across task subsets — compare on the subset you care about.
Compare only like with like: scores from different leaderboards are not comparable, and neither are different eval settings (context length, tools on/off) within one.
Ask whether the gap is meaningful: 1–2 points is usually within eval noise; adjacent ranks are effectively a tie.
Fill the gap with your own eval: public leaderboards answer "general level"; your own 20–50 questions answer "is it good at my job".

提示词怎么版本化.lead: If you can't say which change moved your live numbers, it's usually because prompts live inside code and get edited on the fly. The minimal way to treat prompts like code.
points: Move prompts out of code strings into their own files: editing a prompt shouldn't require a rebuild or redeploy.
Commit every change with the motivation written down: traceable, diffable, revertable — just like code.
Pair changes with a regression run: fixed inputs, old vs new outputs; without an eval, "improved" is a feeling.
Record prompt and model version as a pair: the same prompt can break on a new model; log them together.
When production misbehaves, check the prompt changelog first: prompts are a common change source that rarely sits inside the audit trail.
Control variables in A/B comparisons: swap prompt and model together and you'll never know which one did it.

系统提示怎么设计.lead: A system prompt is the invisible spec of your product's behavior. What to put in it, what to leave out, and how to test whether it actually holds.
points: Standing rules only: identity, tone, boundaries, refusal policy. One-off tasks go in the user message — don't mix them in.
Write checkable clauses: "cite a link when quoting external information" beats "be honest" — it's enforceable and testable one by one.
Give boundary clauses an exit: refuse with a reason plus an alternative; a bare "don't do X" yields robotic refusals.
A system prompt is not a security boundary: a motivated user can always get around it; the real defenses sit in permissions and tools.
Test clause by clause: each rule gets one should-trigger and one should-not-trigger input; re-run on every revision.
Version it like a prompt: system-prompt edits need model-version records and regression runs too.

换模型前怎么迁移评估.lead: Switching models is not renaming: the same prompt set can break on the new one. Four checks to pass before you switch.
points: Run your own eval on old vs new first: public leaderboards show general level; only your real inputs say whether the switch works.
Diff the API surface item by item: parameter names, streaming behavior, structured-output support, context length — a compatible interface is not identical behavior.
Re-test everything that depends on prompts: the same prompt can behave very differently across models; boundary clauses drift most.
Check licenses and data terms: the new model's license, data-retention policy, and regional availability may differ from the old one.
Keep a rollback path: retain the old model's configuration until the confirmation window closes, so you can switch back with one click.
Close out with live metrics during the confirmation window: task completion, refusal rate, and cost against baseline — retire the old model only when they pass.

数据标注与质检怎么看.lead: "We used a million annotated rows" says nothing about quality. How to size up a training or eval dataset from three angles: who labeled it, how consistent they were, and how QA ran.
points: Start with who did the labeling: crowdworkers, in-house staff, or domain experts — unit price is usually a good proxy for data quality.
Check inter-annotator agreement: low agreement on the same batch means the guidelines themselves are ambiguous, so the noise is real.
QA process beats label count: sampling rate, rework loop, and disagreement arbitration — miss any of the three and the scale number is hollow.
"What counts as correct" must be written into the annotation guidelines: vague rules make annotators guess, and guessed data trains a wobbly model.
Model-labeled data (synthetic data, AI feedback) is not exempt: it carries the labeling model's biases; at minimum add human spot-checks plus eval regression.
Data problems surface in evals eventually: when model behavior gets weird, audit the latest batch's guideline changes before touching hyperparameters.

怎么读一篇AI论文.lead: Not being able to get through a paper is usually a sequencing problem, not an English problem. This guide is the order to read an AI paper in, and the question each step should answer.
points: Find the research question first: the one or two sentences in the intro saying what the paper sets out to solve. If you can't find it, the paper itself isn't clear — read on cautiously.

Treat the abstract as a table of contents, not a conclusion: NeurIPS's official checklist makes authors self-audit whether 'the main claims in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper's contributions and scope' — an abstract is a promise; the evidence lives in the tables.

Locate the main evidence: first answer 'which table/figure does the headline claim rest on', then check that table's setup — which benchmark, which baseline, which metric — and only then look at the numbers.

Read the limitations section directly: the NeurIPS checklist also asks authors to describe limitations. What authors admit themselves is the boundary of applicability — more reliable than any third-party take.
Separate 'new method' from 'good results': ablations are what show which component actually matters; without ablations, the source of the gain is unknown.
Citation counts, conference acceptance, and launch buzz are not evidence of quality; on seeing a SOTA claim, check benchmark contamination first, then whether the comparison is apples-to-apples.

论文卡-Attention Is All You Need.lead: The source paper of the Transformer. This card lays out the question it set out to solve, where the evidence lives, and what the paper does not claim.
points: Research question: can sequence transduction work with attention alone — the abstract's "dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely".

Core evidence: Section 4 and Table 1 compare three architectures on path length, per-layer compute, and sequential operations; experiments are two machine-translation tasks, 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 EN-DE (abstract).

Author-stated limitations: the paper has no standalone Limitations section (verified against the arXiv HTML version on 2026-10-29); Section 7's attention visualizations explain the mechanism, not the limits — applicability is the reader's job.

What it does not claim: the paper never says this architecture will train general-purpose language models. "Transformer is the foundation of LLMs" is our retrospective framing, not the paper's conclusion.
Reading tip: the three-way complexity comparison in Table 1 is the actual argument; looking only at the architecture diagram misses the claim.

论文卡-GPT-3.lead: The starting point of the 'big model' narrative. This card separates what the paper actually demonstrated, what the authors themselves flagged as limits, and which popular claims are not in the paper.
points: Research question: pre-train + fine-tune needs task-specific labeled data, yet humans learn new language tasks from a few examples or instructions — can a model learn tasks from context without updating weights (abstract).

Core evidence: the Section 3 tables organized by task family (language modeling, closed-book QA, translation, commonsense, SuperGLUE…). The claim is one model, no fine-tuning, many tasks — check baselines and settings table by table.
Author-stated limitations (Section 5, verified): "it still has notable weaknesses in text synthesis and several NLP tasks".
The words 'emergent abilities' / 'emergence' do not appear in the paper (full-text check on 2026-10-29) — that framing comes from later papers.
What it does not claim: the paper does not claim the model 'understands' language, and 'scale always delivers' is not its wording either — its claims are strictly about few-shot task performance.

论文卡-InstructGPT.lead: The landmark paper that moved 'alignment' into mainstream training. This card pins down the question, the key numbers, and where the authors list their own limitations.
points: Research question: the abstract opens with "Making language models bigger does not inherently make them better at following a user's intent" — bigger models can be untruthful, toxic, or simply unhelpful.

Core evidence: labelers prefer outputs from the 1.3B InstructGPT to the 175B GPT-3 — "despite having 100x fewer parameters" (abstract). Alignment quality decouples from parameter count; this is the paper's hardest result.

Author-stated limitations: Section 5 (the HTML version contains 5.3 limitations / 5.4 open questions / 5.5 broader impacts); the abstract itself says toxicity improved only slightly and bias not at all.
Key line for evaluation readers (abstract): "Public NLP datasets are not reflective of how our language models are used" — this directly supports our 'How to Read a Leaderboard' stance.
What it does not claim: RLHF did not solve hallucination or bias — the paper says so; 'alignment = safer' cannot be inferred from this paper either.

论文卡-Chinchilla.lead: The calibration paper on 'how big should the model be, how much data should it see'. This card quotes the conclusion, states the evidence scale, and notes the extrapolation boundary the authors themselves flag.
points: Research question (abstract): under a fixed compute budget, what is the optimal model size and token count; the finding is that current LLMs are "significantly undertrained" because the field scaled models while keeping data constant.

Conclusion verbatim: "for compute-optimal training, the model size and the number of training tokens should be scaled equally: for every doubling of model size the number of training tokens should also be doubled".
Evidence scale: 400+ models trained (70M to 16B+ parameters, 5B to 500B tokens) to fit the scaling law, then validated with the 70B Chinchilla, which "outperforms Gopher" (Section 4.2, verified).

Author-flagged boundary (verified): Chinchilla trained on 4× more data than Gopher, and the authors warn train/test leakage may artificially boost results — even a calibration paper guards against contamination.

What it does not claim: the law is fitted on ≤16B models and extrapolated — 'the rule holds past 70B' is extrapolation, not measurement; 'parameter count doesn't matter' is not the paper's claim either.

论文卡-HELM.lead: The evaluation-framework paper behind 'don't trust a single score'. This card lays out the question, how the framework is built, and the trade-offs the authors declare.
points: Research question (abstract): LMs' "capabilities, limitations, and risks are not well understood"; HELM aims at transparency, not at crowning a strongest model.

Framework: taxonomize scenarios (use cases) and metrics (desiderata), select a subset by coverage and feasibility, and state what is missing (the abstract names QA for neglected English dialects and trustworthiness metrics) — admitting coverage gaps is part of the method.

Core approach verbatim: measure 7 metrics (accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, efficiency) across 16 core scenarios where possible, "ensuring metrics beyond accuracy don't fall to the wayside".
Declared trade-off: broad, not exhaustive — cite HELM together with its scenario list; a HELM ranking detached from scenarios is meaningless.
What it does not claim: HELM is not a replacement leaderboard — it opposes single-metric ranking itself; 'ranked first on HELM' contradicts the paper's stance.

论文卡-Llama 2.lead: The landmark tech report for open-weight chat models. This card lays out what it set out to solve, where the evidence sits, and what it does not claim.
points: Research question: the abstract announces "a collection of pretrained and fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) ranging in scale from 7 billion to 70 billion parameters"; the fine-tuned Llama 2-Chat is "optimized for dialogue use cases".

Core evidence: Section 3's fine-tuning pipeline (SFT + rejection sampling + PPO) and Section 4's safety work — the abstract itself frames the contribution as "We provide a detailed description of our approach to fine-tuning and safety improvements"; the comparison claim carries a qualifier: "outperform open-source chat models on most benchmarks we tested" (most, not all).

Author-stated limits: no standalone Limitations section (checked against the arXiv HTML version on 2026-10-29); the closest are Section 5 Discussion (trade-offs and risks) and Section 4 Safety (with a content warning) — discussion, not a limitations list. Scope of validity is the reader's job.

What it does not claim: the abstract says "may be a suitable substitute for closed-source models" — never a claim of surpassing them. And open-weight is not open-source: the community license carries use restrictions (see the Open weights term).
How to read it: the core contribution is the openness of the fine-tuning and safety process, not the benchmark scores; reading only the eval tables misses what the paper actually gives.

论文卡-LIMA.lead: The 'less is more' alignment-data experiment: fine-tuning on just 1,000 curated examples. This card lays out what it set out to test, where the evidence sits, and what it does not claim.
points: Research question: the abstract describes training LIMA (a 65B LLaMa model) "fine-tuned with the standard supervised loss on only 1,000 carefully curated prompts and responses", "without any reinforcement learning or human preference modeling" — the point is to measure the relative importance of the two training stages.

Core evidence: Section 4's human evaluation (against GPT-4, Bard, DaVinci003) and Section 5's ablations on data diversity/quality/quantity — the abstract gives the controlled human-study number: "responses from LIMA are either equivalent or strictly preferred to GPT-4 in 43% of cases"; the conclusion line is "almost all knowledge in large language models is learned during pretraining".

Author-stated limits: no standalone Limitations section (checked against the arXiv HTML version on 2026-10-30); Section 7's Discussion states two limits outright — the mental effort of building such examples is hard to scale, and "LIMA is not as robust as product-grade models" (an unlucky decode or an adversarial prompt often yields a weak response).

What it does not claim: 43%/58%/65% are shares of "equivalent or strictly preferred" in a controlled human study — not "matches GPT-4 overall"; "1,000 examples suffice" is evidence about dialogue style, not about safety, factuality, or robustness — the very areas the authors admit are weak.

How to read it: its value is turning the hypothesis "knowledge comes from pretraining, alignment data shapes style" into testable ablations; when citing it, separate "little data can align a model" from "little data can align everything".

论文卡-Self-Instruct.lead: The founding framework for synthetic instruction data: models generate the instructions that train them. This card lays out what it set out to solve, where the evidence sits, and what it does not claim.
points: Research question: the abstract notes instruction-tuned models "depend heavily on human-written instruction data that is often limited in quantity, diversity, and creativity"; the fix is Self-Instruct — "improving the instruction-following capabilities of pretrained language models by bootstrapping off their own generations".

Core evidence: Section 2's method (generate instructions, inputs, and outputs; filter invalid or near-duplicate samples; fine-tune the original model; seeded from 175 human-annotated tasks) and Section 4's results — applied to vanilla GPT3, "a 33% absolute improvement over the original model on Super-NaturalInstructions", "on par with the performance of InstructGPT-001", which was trained on private user data and human annotations.

Author-stated limits: a standalone Section 8 Limitations exists (checked against the arXiv HTML version on 2026-10-30), naming three: tail phenomena (gains skew toward tasks frequent in the pretraining corpus, brittleness on uncommon or creative instructions), dependence on large models (may work best for big models, raising access barriers), and reinforcing the model's own biases (the iterative loop can amplify problematic social biases).

What it does not claim: the abstract says on par, and the human eval leaves "only a 5% absolute gap behind InstructGPT-001" — never a claim of surpassing it; and "almost annotation-free" is not zero annotation: the 175 seed tasks and the filtering rules are still human-designed.

How to read it: this is the source of the "synthesize data to train yourself" line — many later instruction datasets and self-improvement methods reuse its generate-and-filter skeleton. Separate the reusable method from the specific GPT3 numbers, which move a lot with base-model capability.

Agent 评估怎么做.lead: Agent success is not only the final answer: whether tools were chosen correctly, arguments were right, how many steps it took and what it cost all belong in the eval.
points: Define task success first: not "a plausible answer" but "goal achieved + correct tool calls + no overreach".
Record the full trajectory: messages, tool calls, arguments, return values, steps, latency and tokens; without it you cannot attribute failure.
Score four things separately: final answer, tool choice, argument correctness and process efficiency (steps and cost).
Across repeated runs, record success rate and failure types. pass@k concerns at least one success, not success every time. For repeatability, explicitly report an all-k-success metric.
Calculate input, output and tool charges for each call, then sum steps and retries. Do not multiply already aggregated tokens by the step count again.
Build a regression set: put production failures into a fixed question set and rerun after every model or prompt change.

上下文工程怎么做.lead: Context engineering is not "stuff more material in". It decides what the model sees each turn, what it does not see, and how to compress the rest.
points: Fix the must-haves first: current goal, hard constraints, available tools, output format and one or two examples; everything else is optional.
Drop irrelevant history and repeated tool output: if the same file was read three times, keep the latest read and the diff.
Compress with summaries or structured state: turn a long conversation into "confirmed facts / open tasks / unresolved questions" rather than truncating verbatim.
Govern tool output: paginate, truncate, extract only relevant passages and keep source references instead of pasting whole pages.
Draw memory boundaries: in-session state, cross-session facts and external retrieval are three layers; do not treat retrieval results as memory.
Acceptance looks at two numbers: task success rate up and tokens per turn down; only both count as effective.

RAG 全链路：从文档到答案.lead: Parsing, chunking, embedding, retrieval, reranking, generation and citation — every step fails on its own. This guide strings them into a debuggable pipeline.
points: Document parsing and chunking: handle layout, tables and scans first, then cut on semantic boundaries and keep headings and provenance; parse wrong and everything downstream is wrong.
Embedding and index: record model version and dimensions; changing the embedding model means rebuilding the index.
Retrieval: recall enough candidates first, then narrow with a reranker or rules; top-1 alone misses too much.
Assemble context: include only relevant chunks with source labels; deduplicate chunks so the same passage does not consume tokens twice.
Generation and citation: require each answer sentence to map to a source; mark unsourced sentences as inference.
Agentic RAG: let the agent rewrite queries, decide whether to retrieve again and judge whether material is sufficient; the price is more steps and cost.
Evaluate separately: recall, answer correctness and citation correctness, not just the final answer.

2026 评测基准地图.lead: Leaderboards are not truth, but different benchmarks measure different abilities. This map groups coding, agents, long context, multimodal and safety, with a reading checklist.
points: Coding: HumanEval is dated; the SWE-bench family is closer to real repository work. Check the Verified subset and version.
Agents: τ-bench, AgentBench and Terminal-Bench measure multi-step tasks and tool use. Check the task set, tool surface and number of runs.
Long context: RULER and LongBench measure retrieval and reasoning over long inputs. Check length tiers and middle-of-context behaviour.
Multimodal: MMMU measures university-level image-text reasoning and Video-MME measures video understanding. Check modality coverage and protocol.
Safety and alignment: refusal, jailbreak, bias and red-team benchmarks exist, but a single score cannot replace your own acceptance test.
Six questions for any leaderboard: version, training cutoff, public task set, decontamination, pass@k versus single run, and whether cost/steps are disclosed.
Conclusion: benchmarks narrow the candidates; they do not decide for you. Run your own task set before shipping.

量化、蒸馏、剪枝的区别.lead: All three routes make a model smaller, but they touch different things: quantisation lowers precision, distillation swaps in a student, pruning removes structure.
points: Quantisation: lower weights from FP16 to 4/8 bit while keeping the architecture; VRAM drops, quality depends on the tier and calibration data.
Distillation: train a small student on a large teacher’s outputs; you change the model, not the precision.
Pruning: remove weights, channels or layers; it needs retraining/fine-tuning and the structure really shrinks.
Costs differ: quantisation is easiest but may lose quality; distillation needs data and compute; pruning needs retraining and may damage capability.
Order: distil to a smaller model, then quantise for deployment; after pruning, fine-tune, then quantise.
Acceptance: compare quality, VRAM, latency and cost on the same task set; do not compare size alone.

AI 常见误区总索引.lead: An index of misconceptions — more parameters is smarter, bigger context is better, a high leaderboard score means usable — each pointing to its explanation.
points: More parameters is smarter: scale interacts with data, architecture and task; a single number is not enough.
Bigger context is better: context has VRAM and latency costs, and middle-of-input use is uneven.
Higher temperature is smarter: temperature changes sampling randomness, not what the model knows.
A high leaderboard score means usable: benchmarks have version, contamination and task-mismatch problems; run your own task set.
Quantisation halves intelligence / not enough VRAM means it cannot run: quality depends on tier and calibration; low VRAM can use CPU offload, multi-GPU splitting or a smaller member.
Open models are always cheaper / preview builds cannot be used in production: hardware, power, operations and time all count; check the specific product terms.
API compatibility means behaviour matches / switching models is just a rename: protocol compatibility is not output semantics; prompts, tools and evals all need realignment.

2026 下半年变化线.lead: Official update snapshots: distinguish dates, rollout scope and planned shutdowns, with source references.
points: Research: Google shipped Deep Research and Deep Research Max on 2026-04-21, built on Gemini 3.1 Pro with MCP and custom sources.
Image: Nano Banana 2 (Gemini 3.1 Flash Image) launched on 2026-02-26 with generation and editing.
Retirements: the ChatGPT Atlas browser was retired on 2026-08-09 with capabilities moved into ChatGPT/Codex; Microsoft retired consumer Copilot Deep Research on 2026-08-18.
Model tiers: Gemini 4 Argon rollout for AI Pro/Ultra began on 2026-10-13; Claude Duet opened a Pro/Max research preview on 2026-10-21.
Tools: Opal is scheduled to shut down on 2026-11-17 without automatic workflow migration; preserve prompts and files. Vercel AI SDK 7 appears in its 2026 changelog.
Local: ExLlamaV3 1.6.5 was released on 2026-10-25 (PyPI); the models snapshot is dated 2026-10-30.
How to read it: check the date first, then the tier; for retirements, follow where the capability moved.

怎么写一份能被复核的任务指令.lead: Turn "help me with this" into an instruction others can check: spell out the goal, the inputs, the boundaries, and what counts as passing.
points: Fill in four fields: goal (what must be delivered), inputs (which materials it gets), boundaries (what it must not do), acceptance (what counts as passing). Missing any one leaves the reviewer guessing at your intent.
Write acceptance as a decidable sentence: not "good quality", but "every conclusion points back to a specific location in the source material".
Boundaries need prohibitions and exception handling: facts not found in the material get marked "not found", not filled in from common sense.
Make the output carry its own evidence: material IDs used, tools called, parts left undone - the reviewer checks against exactly these.

Worked example (fictional scenario): input is 12 pages of support tickets -> processing produces "issue category + paragraph reference" from a template -> the check is to sample 5 items and confirm the category matches the cited paragraph -> if they do not match, the next step is to tighten the boundary wording in the category definitions and rerun, not to swap models.
Version the brief itself: log one line on "why this changed", or in six months nobody knows which acceptance rule still applies.

怎么搭一条最小评测流程.lead: You do not need dozens of benchmarks. A usable evaluation pipeline needs five things: samples, criteria, judgment method, records, reruns.
points: Collect 20-50 samples from your own work and note where each came from; this tracks your usage better than copying a public benchmark. Hold some samples back from prompt tuning and use them only to compare before and after.
Phrase criteria as questions a person can answer directly: not "is this answer good", but "does it cite a deadline that the material never states".
Split judgment into two tiers: run scripts over what machines can decide (fields present, citation IDs that really exist); route the rest to humans and record how much needed a human.
Keep records you can revisit: model version, prompt version, sample-set version, date, per-item outcome and reason. Skip one field and the next round is not comparable.
Rerun the same sample set whenever any single piece changes; run one input two or three times to see the spread - the variance is part of the record.

Worked example (fictional data): input is 30 contract-clause Q&A samples -> processing checks citation existence by script and conclusion correctness by hand -> result this round: 24/30 passed (a made-up count, not a measured result) -> next step: first separate missing citations from wrong judgments; fix retrieval or prompt for the former, fix the acceptance rule for the latter, not both at once.
Samples age: when user phrasing or the policy text changes, add new samples and relabel part of the old set, otherwise the pipeline keeps measuring the past.

怎么处理一次误发事故.lead: Treat a misfire (a wrong answer in a customer email, wrong code merged to main) as an incident: stop the bleeding, scope it, then review - do not start with blame.
points: Step one is containment, not analysis: retract or correct what went out, close the triggering entry point, list what has spread. Analysis comes second.

Scope must rest on evidence: time window, list of affected users or files, whether anything was published externally. If you cannot produce a list, write "scope unknown" instead of estimating a number.
Preserve evidence: original input, model and prompt versions, full output, the call logs of that moment, filed under an incident ID. Every later judgement depends on these.

Attribute by layer: model output wrong, retrieved material wrong, the instruction itself ambiguous, or no review step in the process - the same symptom has four different fixes, so do not assume it is the model.

The review must land on "which control changes": add a review point, tighten permissions, write the scenario into the boundary notes or the sample set - each with an owner and a verification method, not "be more careful".

Worked example (fictional scenario): input is an automated reply that sent a customer the wrong refund deadline -> processing closes the automated-reply channel first, then counts the send log for the same window -> the check compares the output against current refund terms and finds the retrieval hit an outdated policy document -> next step: put policy document versions into the release check, add a deadline-field validation at the exit, and record how you will verify it.

怎么给 AI 内容加来源标识.lead: Provenance has three layers: the visible notice, the credentials inside the file, and the generator-side watermark. Here is where each is added and where each gets lost.
points: Fix the position of the visible label first: text and images state it in the body or on the image, audio and video say it at the start or on screen. A single line in a page corner can miss both readers and reviewers.

Implicit labels live in file metadata: content credentials such as C2PA record who generated it, with which tool, and which steps changed it - but transcoding, screenshots and re-export can strip them entirely.

Separate generator watermarks from your own labeling: model-side marks (for example SynthID) are injected by the generating party, do not cover your later edits, and cannot replace the notice you owe.

Check obligations against the text of the rule: China's labeling Measures set separate requirements for explicit and implicit labels; scope and exceptions follow the article and how your service is classified.
Build one checklist per content type: what label an image, video, audio or text needs, which stage adds it, which step verifies it - a missing cell means a whole batch slips through.

Worked example (fictional flow): input is an AI-generated event poster -> processing writes content credentials at generation and overlays a visible mark at publish time -> the check downloads the finished file to confirm the credential is still in the metadata and the mark is visible -> if the credential disappears after compression, next step is to move validation to the end of the publishing pipeline and require channels to keep the original file, rather than adding a verbal note.

怎么审一次第三方插件.lead: Before connecting a third-party MCP server or plugin, audit four things: what permissions it asks for, where its code comes from, where data goes, and who owns an incident.
points: List the permissions: which directories it reads, whether it can make network calls, whether it can execute commands. Permissions beyond the stated purpose get cut, or the plugin does not get connected.
Look at code provenance and maintenance: repository ownership, recent commits, whether security issues in the tracker get responses - these say more than a star count.
Ask three questions about data flow: do logs store prompt content, is anything sent back to the vendor, is it used for training. If the answers are unclear, treat it as "data leaves".
Run it in isolation first: separate account, minimal permissions, test data only, with tool-call logs kept somewhere you can actually query.

Test for injection: put a line saying "ignore previous instructions" into a tool description or a tool response and see whether it executes - indirect prompt injection usually arrives through tool output, not user input.
Define the exit plan: which places to change when replacing it, how to clear historical data, who approves. A connection without an exit plan writes the dependency into your architecture.

Worked example (fictional flow): input is a filesystem server claiming to "only read the project README" -> processing gives it one directory in a sandbox and disables network access -> the check looks at whether it touched only that directory and whether logs stayed local -> if it requests a path outside the directory, next step is to revoke access and file it against an OWASP LLM risk category, not merely lower permissions and keep using it.

怎么设计人工复核环节.lead: Human review is not "add a person who clicks confirm"; it is a step where someone can see the error, can block it, and carries a named responsibility.
points: Set the trigger conditions first: money, external publication, irreversible actions, or cases where the model flags its own uncertainty go to review; everything else should not consume human attention.

Show reviewers comparison material, not just conclusions: source text beside the generated text, citation IDs, and the parts the model says it is unsure about. Hand over only a conclusion and review degrades into a rubber stamp.
Define the available actions: edit, reject, escalate. If the workflow offers only an "approve" button, the rejection rate stays at zero and the metric carries no information.

Guard against automation bias: long streaks of quick approvals mean people stopped looking. Sampling review quality (disagreement between reviewers, items later corrected) tells you more than sampling model output alone.
Track three numbers per task type: review time, rejection rate, distribution of rejection reasons. Use them to work back to whether the prompt is vague or the acceptance standard is unclear.

Worked example (fictional scenario): input is a model-written "summary of breach clauses in a contract" -> processing has the reviewer check three key statements against the source and mark "consistent / inconsistent / unsure", citing the paragraph -> the rule is: inconsistent gets rejected with the basis paragraph noted, unsure escalates to legal -> if two categories in a row come back inconsistent, next step is to default that task type back to human drafting and then fix the prompt and retrieval, rather than asking reviewers to check harder.

怎么给团队做 AI 风险清单.lead: A risk list is not "safety" written as a slogan; per use case it states what could go wrong, what already blocks it, and who closes the rest.
points: Break it down by use case, not by model: the same model drafting weekly reports and issuing automatic refunds carries different risks, so one row cannot cover both.
Fill five cells per entry: scenario, trigger condition, consequence, controls in place, remaining gap. A list with only the first two cells drives no action.
Borrow an existing taxonomy as the skeleton, then add yours: NIST AI RMF's Govern / Map / Measure / Manage and OWASP's LLM risk categories beat starting from a blank page.

Keep regulatory risks in their own column with the article and effective conditions noted (the EU AI Act tiers by use; China's Measures turn on service type); do not mix them with experience issues in one table.
Set update triggers and owners: connecting a new model, a new data source, or a process change should force another pass. Entries nobody owns count as not written.

Worked example (fictional scenario): input is the use case "AI drafts customer replies" -> processing fills the five cells with trigger conditions "refund deadlines, compensation, legal wording" -> the check reviews existing controls and finds no deadline-field validation at the exit, so the gap stands -> next step: turn the gap into a to-do with an owner and a verification method (for example a weekly sample audit of replies, sample size set by your own volume rather than copied from someone else's threshold).

怎么读模型卡与系统卡.lead: Model cards say what a model is and how to use it; system cards and deployment safety pages say what was tested before release and what still worries the publisher. Read them separately, and side by side.
points: Tell the two apart by audience: model cards face users (intended use, limitations, evaluation scope, training-data notes); system cards and deployment safety pages face risk readers (which risks were measured, with what result, under what conditions the rollout continues).

Check what was measured and what was not: a document with only capability benchmarks and no failure-mode discussion cannot support a high-risk use; one that only discusses risk without checkable numbers is no better.
Record version and date together: results for the same model name can differ across card releases, so put the version and publication date in your notes when you cite it.
Read the "not suitable for" section closely: failure cases and refusal behaviour the publisher writes down are more usable than marketing lines; a card without that section deserves discount.
Map gaps onto your own use: if your scenario is outside its evaluation coverage, that gap is yours to test - extrapolation does not fill it.

Worked example (fictional need): input is a team wanting a model to draft medical Q&A answers -> processing reads the model card and system card side by side and lists "is there any medical evaluation" and "which section states known refusals and hallucination behaviour" -> the judgement is that if neither document covers the scenario, the conclusion reads "cards insufficient to support this use" -> next step: add the scenario to your own evaluation samples, run a small trial with records, then decide whether to integrate.

怎么估算一次上线的安全成本.lead: Split "safety cost" into labour, compute, review and rework, and estimate each with numbers you can look up - or with assumptions labelled as assumptions.
points: List spending items, not adjectives: sample preparation, review rounds, parallel running during a staged rollout, rework windows, rollback drills - each with who does it and how often.

Take the base from your own history: handling time for comparable tasks, rejection rate, ticket volume. If the data is missing, write "assumed value" and keep the assumption plus its reason in the sheet instead of a bare number.
Separate one-off from recurring: reading cards and designing permissions are one-off; sampling, monitoring and log retention recur monthly.
Leave room for uncertainty: state which items have wide ranges and why (new scenario, no history, external approval dependency) instead of applying one blanket buffer factor.

Make the "cost of not doing it" traceable: incident handling time, contractual penalty terms, regulatory remediation requirements - each with a source. Leave the cell blank rather than inventing a figure.

Worked example (fictional data): input is a launch of AI-generated support summaries at "300 items a day" (fictional premise) -> processing lists the four items, with sampling at 10% (30 items a day, assumed 2 minutes each) -> the check substitutes the assumptions to get roughly one hour of human work per day and compares it against capacity to decide whether to narrow scope -> if capacity is exceeded, next step is to state plainly either the risk of lowering the sampling rate or the reduced first-batch scope, rather than writing an assumption into the plan as a commitment.

怎么把安全要求写进采购条款.lead: Procurement clauses turn what you care about into what the supplier must deliver: documents, notices, logs and exit - four levers.
points: Make document delivery concrete: require model cards or system cards and usage documentation, with version numbers and publication dates. "See our website" is not a deliverable.
State change-notice conditions and lead time: model replacement, data-retention changes, subprocessor changes each get a point in the process and a notification method.
Write data flow into the clause: log retention period, whether data trains models, whether processing can stay in a chosen region, and the deadline and format for export and deletion.
Define incident obligations by what evidence you can obtain: notification duties, which logs you can export as evidence, how responsibility and remediation are assigned.

Give exit real teeth: export formats for data and configuration, proof of deletion after termination, disposition of historical records. A connection without exit terms writes the dependency into your architecture.

Hand regulatory wording to legal: how the AI Act's staged duties and China's Measures and labeling rules land on your business is their call; the clause only states who bears which duty and who produces the proof.

Worked example (fictional clause): input is a draft contract that only promises "a high-quality model" -> processing replaces it clause by clause with the four levers (versioned documents, change notice with agreed lead time, logs not used for training and exportable, deletion proof with deadlines) -> the check asks on the spot "which logs can I obtain to prove inputs and outputs after an incident"; no answer means a clause gap -> next step: turn the gaps into a list for legal and the vendor to work through, rather than accepting a verbal promise.

评测分数高就等于可靠.lead: A score answers "how many points on that set"; reliability asks "what happens when I use it repeatedly".
评测分数高就等于可靠.myth: A high evaluation score means the system is reliable in use.
评测分数高就等于可靠.fact: Reliability is about spread and distribution: whether the same input gives consistent results over repeats, how unseen inputs behave, what failures look like at the boundaries. A score is one reading of one version on one task set under one setting - a different question. Judge reliability by rerunning your own samples and recording the variance. (Fictional example) Input is one query about a refund deadline -> processing runs it three times with the same prompt and the same model version -> the check finds one of the three stating the deadline wrongly, so variance on this path is not zero -> the next step is to add that phrasing to your own sample set and recheck after a fix, not to cite the high score.

加了护栏就安全了.lead: Guardrails change the default path, not every path.
加了护栏就安全了.myth: Turn on the vendor's guardrails and the system is safe.
加了护栏就安全了.fact: Guardrails mainly cover common paths anticipated during training and deployment. Content routed around them - reworded inducements, instructions hidden in tool output or web page text - plus the guardrails' own boundaries still depend on your permission design, exit validation and incident process. Verifying that guardrails actually work means a reproducible check (fictional example): input an untrusted text carrying an instruction -> processing runs it through the real chain -> the check looks at whether that instruction executed or environment variables were read -> if it executed, the next step is to tighten tool permissions and add exit filtering, not to treat "guardrails enabled" as the conclusion.

通过一次评测就可以上线.lead: Shipping is not passing one exam; it is a state that needs continuous checking.
通过一次评测就可以上线.myth: Run the evaluation once before launch and you never have to look again.
通过一次评测就可以上线.fact: That single pass covers only the version combination at the time: model version, prompt, retrieved material, user phrasing and data distribution - a change in any of them can void the result. After release keep sampling, monitoring and a rollback path, and rerun the same sample set on changes. (Fictional example) Input is a change that swaps only the retrieval source, with model and prompt untouched -> processing reruns the previous sample set -> the check looks at the single criterion "does the citation hit the current document" -> if that pass rate drops, the next step is to redo the go-live decision and add a retrieval-source change check, not to keep relying on last round's "passed".

本地部署就等于合规.lead: Keeping data on your own machines addresses where data flows, not what obligations apply.
本地部署就等于合规.myth: Deploy the model locally and compliance is automatically solved.
本地部署就等于合规.fact: Compliance follows the business, not the location of the compute: intended use, who the service faces, the authorisation chain for the data, content labeling and record keeping. Local deployment adds its own items - weight and license terms, which internal data gets connected, and who is allowed to use which model. What to verify is how the service is classified and which duties still apply, not whether the machine is yours. (Fictional example) Input is the decision to move the same externally facing summarisation service from cloud to a local model -> processing still checks three things: who the service faces, whether published generated content needs labeling, and how far the internal data authorisation reaches -> if any one of them still applies, the conclusion "local deployment, therefore no duties" is wrong -> the next step is to have legal confirm the classification and to write the labeling practice into the release check. Final obligations follow the text of the rule.

论文卡-Constitutional AI.lead: A training method that treats a human-written list of principles as the source of supervision. This card states what it set out to solve, which conclusions the abstract supports, and what it does not claim.
points: Research question (abstract's opening): "we would like to enlist their help to supervise other AIs" - the target is "training a harmless AI assistant through self-improvement", achieved "without any human labels identifying harmful outputs"; "The only human oversight is provided through a list of rules or principles", which is why the authors name it Constitutional AI.

Where the method sits (two phases as the abstract describes them): the supervised phase is to "generate self-critiques and revisions" and then "finetune the original model on revised responses"; the RL phase compares two samples with a model, trains a preference model from AI preferences and uses it as the reward signal - the abstract calls this "RL from AI Feedback" (RLAIF). Experimental values and settings appear nowhere in the abstract.

What the abstract's own conclusion says: the result is "a harmless but non-evasive AI assistant that engages with harmful queries by explaining its objections to them", and both phases can use chain-of-thought style reasoning to improve human-judged performance and transparency of AI decision making. The closing phrase "with far fewer human labels" is about the volume of labels and controllability, not a safety guarantee. The abstract carries no separate limitations section; limitations live in the body, and this check covered only the arXiv abstract page.

What it does not claim: that the method removes harmful outputs, and that "using Constitutional AI" equals safety. The principle list is written by people - what it includes and what it omits is still a human judgement, unverified at the abstract level.

How to read it (fictional need): read it as "supervision source replaced by rule text", not as a certificate. Input is a scenario with requests that must be refused and explained -> processing asks per rule whether it can be written as an executable principle or needs runtime interception -> the judgement is that anything only stoppable at runtime falls outside this method's coverage -> next step: put those items into your own review and incident workflow instead of citing "we use Constitutional AI" as evidence.

论文卡-Distilling the Knowledge.lead: Compressing the judgement of several models into one easier-to-deploy model - an early short paper on distillation. This card states the question, where the conclusions stop, and what it does not claim.
points: Research question (abstract): averaging many models trained on the same data helps, but predicting with a whole ensemble "is cumbersome and may be too computationally expensive to allow deployment to a large number of users"; building on Caruana and collaborators, the authors "compress the knowledge in an ensemble into a single model which is much easier to deploy".

Where the evidence sits: the abstract gives only qualitative claims - "we achieve some surprising results on MNIST" and "we can significantly improve the acoustic model of a heavily used commercial system by distilling the knowledge in an ensemble of models into a single model". Values, model sizes and settings are in the body's experiments; nothing quotable numerically appears in the abstract.

What else it introduces: a new ensemble form - one or more full models plus many specialist models that learn to separate fine-grained classes the full models confuse; the abstract sets this apart from a mixture of experts: "these specialist models can be trained rapidly and in parallel".

Limits the authors state: the abstract treats deployment cost as the problem being solved rather than a leftover limitation, and lists no limitations; this check covered the arXiv abstract page, so the body's small experimental scope and failure cases are not restated here.

What it does not claim: that a distilled small model matches the teacher on every task, and that distillation equals quantization or pruning - they act on different layers. Using this paper as proof that "small models are always enough" goes beyond its evidence.

How to read it (fictional need): input is "replace a key-sentence detector with a smaller model" -> processing follows its recipe, training the small model on the existing model's output labels -> the judgement compares misses and false alarms on your own held-out set instead of quoting the paper's MNIST result -> if misses rise noticeably in your scenario, next step is to fall back to "keep the teacher, optimise inference only" and record the basis and date of that decision.
